posts.title: Foundry Row Terrace Drains: Two Weeks in a Confined Street
posts.excerpt: How a 3 t compact excavator completed two weeks of deep drainage excavation within the narrow confines of an Eastmere terraced alley.
posts.content:
Replacing Victorian drainage infrastructure behind terraced housing presents one of the most demanding access challenges in urban groundworks. When a contractor approached Kashidashi Hire to support a drainage replacement along Foundry Row in Eastmere, the physical constraints were obvious from the initial site survey. The narrow rear service alley measured barely two metres across, flanked by high brick garden walls and crossed overhead by domestic service cables. Moving equipment in and out without disturbing boundary masonry required a machine that balanced compact dimensions with sufficient breakout force to dig through compacted clay. The project called for our 3 t compact excavator over an initial two-week hire schedule.

Planning began the previous week when Lucía Ferrer registered the booking at our Ferris Road Works Yard hire desk. Because Foundry Row sits well inside our standard 25 km delivery radius, transport on our low-loader was included in the €520 weekly hire rate. Yard coordinator Imani Okafor scheduled the dispatch from Gate 3 for 06:30 on Monday morning to beat morning commuter traffic. Driver Grace Mensah navigated our low-loader to the end of the terrace, unloaded the excavator onto timber tracking, and walked the perimeter with the contractor's site supervisor. Both parties inspected track tension, cab glass, and hydraulic connections before signing the clipped handover sheet that formalised site possession.

Once on site, the 3 t compact excavator proved ideal for the tight trenching runs required. The zero-tail swing design allowed the operator to slew within the narrow corridor without counterweight impact against brick outbuildings. Digging through dense subsoil and ancient gravel beds to reach the collapsed drain pipes two metres below ground level proceeded without interruption. On Tuesday morning, Lucía Ferrer made the yard's standard check call to verify machine performance, noting that the operator was satisfied with track stability and hydraulic response on the uneven rear alley surface.

To maintain preventive standards throughout multi-week jobs, our workshop lead Kenji Arai visited Foundry Row on Wednesday. Performing a scheduled midweek inspection, Kenji checked hydraulic hose lines, lubricated main pin bushings, and inspected bucket teeth for excessive wear against hidden masonry debris. This direct mechanical support from our own depot ensured that minor adjustments were resolved immediately on site, preventing the downtime that often derails tight residential street works.

As the first week concluded, the site team evaluated progress against the required drainage run. Under our yard policy, contractors wishing to extend a hire must confirm by 15:00 on Thursday. Because the groundworks required an additional week of backfilling and aggregate compaction, the supervisor called the hire desk to lock in the second week. Ruth Halvorsen confirmed the account extension without requiring the machine to return to Eastmere for paperwork, keeping plant continuously operational through the weekend.

Work completed during the second week, with new drainage pipes laid, inspected, and backfilled to specification. On Friday afternoon from 14:00, Grace Mensah returned with the low-loader to Gate 3 at Ferris Road Works Yard. A final joint inspection confirmed that the 3 t excavator was clean, fully refuelled, and undamaged, matching the original Monday condition sheet. Tomasz Wierzbicki's founding principle—disciplined weekly plant hire supported by direct yard maintenance—delivered two uninterrupted weeks of production in one of Eastmere's tightest streets.
